K. M. S. DISSANAYAKE, J.
The Petitioner in the instant application made to this Court under Article 140
of the Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
(hereinafter called and referred to as “the Constitution”), seeks in prayer
thereto, a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Certiorari quashing the decision
of the 3rd Respondent dated 20.06.2024 contained in the document annexed
to the petition marked as A2(R3); a mandate in the nature of writ of
Mandamus compelling the 1st and/or 2nd Respondent and/or their servants,
agents and/or any person acting under their authority, the release of
Constine Shavin Sothirajah (hereinafter called and referred to as “the
Detenu”); and a mandate in the nature of a writ of prohibition prohibiting the
1st and/or 2nd Respondent and/or their servants, agents and/or any person
acting under their authority, from detaining the Detenu on the purported
authority of the purported inquiry bearing No. 127/23 (A). On the other hand,
the 1st and 4th Respondents had in their joint statement of objections, prayed
for a dismissal of the instant application with costs in view of the matters
pleaded therein. However, it is to be observed that, the 1st to 4th Respondents
had in their joint written submissions, raised for the first time, a number of
preliminary objections as to the maintainability of the instant application, and
among them the pivotal one, being that, the Petitioner has no locus standi to
institute the instant application.
The facts and the circumstances material and relevant to the instant
application as averred in the petition of the Petitioner, may briefly, be set out
as follows;
The Petitioner being the father of the Detenu seeks in the instant application,
to impugn the alleged illegal detention of his son-the Detenu who is currently,
held in the custody by the 1st and/or 2nd Respondents and/or their servants
and/or theirs agents and any person acting under their authority at the
Colombo Remand Prison; and that according to the Petitioner, the Detenu has
been suffering from a long-standing mental illness resulting in him being
Page 4 of 24
suspected of committing certain crimes which were reported to the Magistrate
Court of Colombo in two cases bearing Nos. 85465/03/23 (to which he had
been admitted to bail) and 79130/05/22, and also to the Magistrate Court of
Kesbewa in case bearing No. 20654 for which he had been in judicial custody
since on or around 15.02.2023 by virtue of the warrants of committals issued
by both the learned Magistrate of Colombo and Kesbewa; and that while, the
Detenu had been held in custody, the Petitioner had sought clinical diagnosis
of the Detenu’s mental health condition from the learned Magistrate of
Kesbewa in pursuant to which learned Magistrate had made an order that
Detenu be clinically, diagnosed by the National Institute of Mental Health;
and that Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist of the National Institute of Mental
Health had by his report dated 20.02.2024 (Y2) submitted to the Magistrate
Court of Kesbewa, stated that Detenu had been diagnosed with a mental
disorder; and that he had to ensure regular follow-ups and be treated for his
mental illness which warrants continuous treatment; and that the learned
Magistrate of Kesbewa had in a detailed order dated 27.05.2024, held that
considering the medical report submitted by the National Institute of Mental
Health, the Detenu should not be held in prison custody, thus, admitting him
to bail by both the Magistrate Court of Kesbewa and Colombo in their
respective orders dated 27.05.2024(Y3) and 26.04.2023 (Y1); and that the
Petitioner had fulfilled all the bail conditions as prescribed in the said orders
and hence, neither the 1st and/or 2nd Respondents and/or their servants
and/or their agents and/or any person acting under their authority nor the
3rd Respondent had any jurisdiction over the Detenu; and that however, the
Detenu had also been accused of attempting to escape from prison custody
from the officers of the Prison Department on or around 22.11.2023 and a
purported inquiry had been initiated before a purported Prison Tribunal; and
that it was evident that the purported Prison Tribunal had concluded the
evidence of a witness in that inquiry; and that on the 20.06.2024, the day on
which the Prison Tribunal had been sitting, Counsel for the Detenu had raised
before it a jurisdictional objection on the premise that the Detenu had been
held in remand custody on the authority of a warrant of committal issued by
Page 5 of 24
the respective Courts in terms of the provisions of the Code of Criminal
Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 and upon being granted bail, and the authority
and/or power granted to them to detain the Detenu in the remand prison by
virtue of the said the warrant of committals issued by the respective Courts,
had become ceased and hence, neither the Prison Tribunal nor the 1st and/or
2nd Respondents and/or their Servants and/or their agents and/or any
person acting under their authority have jurisdiction over the Detenu; and
that the Prison Tribunal in his order dated 20.06.2024(A2/R3) had while
overruling the jurisdictional objection so raised to it, ordered the Detenu to
be held in remand custody and directed the trial to be continued which order
(A2/R3) according to the Petitioner, was unknown to the law; is in breach of
both the Petitioner as well as the Detenu’s rights; was arbitrary, illegal,
unreasonable, irrational and capricious and ultra vires, and hence, the
Detenu has currently, been held in illegal custody by the 1st and/or 2nd
Respondents and/or their Servants and/or their agents and/or any person
acting under their authority on the order of the 3rd Respondent and therefore,
neither of them has any authority in law to hold the detenu in remand custody
and as such their actions were in violation of every norm of a civilized society
and hence, there had been a grave illegality of the action of the Respondents
and grave danger to the life and wellbeing of the Petitioner’s son-the Detenu
hence, the Petitioner was in law, entitled to the relief as prayed for in prayer
to his petition.
Hence, the Petitioner seeks to impugn the order (A2/R3) on the premise that,
a) it was ex facie, a nullity;
b) made without jurisdiction;
c) made with no authority in law;
d) sans any vires.
It is in this context let me, now, closely, examine the order (A2/R3) sought to
be impugned in the instant application by the Petitioner.
Page 6 of 24
The learned Prison Tribunal in the impugned order (A2/R3) had while
overruling the jurisdictional objection so raised to it by the learned Counsel
for the Detenu, held that the Prison Tribunal had jurisdiction under section
81 of the Prisons Ordinance of No. 16 of 1877 as amended (hereinafter called
and referred to as “the Ordinance”) to be read with section 79 thereof, to
detain the Detenu until the final conclusion of the trial already commenced
against him on the charge of attempting to escape from prison custody which
is punishable with an imprisonment and to proceed with the trial towards its
conclusion. It is this order that the Petitioner now, seeks to impugn in the
instant application.
Hence, the pivotal question that would arise for our determination in the
instant application is; Whether the Prison Tribunal has the power and/or
authority and/or jurisdiction vested in it under the Ordinance to remand
ex mero motu a prisoner whose period of detention in the prison custody
determined by a Court of law as envisaged by section 2 of the Ordinance,
has become expired and/or extinct by any means recognized by law, for
the purpose of holding an inquiry and/or continuing with an inquiry
already commenced before the Prison Tribunal into an offence alleged to
have been committed by a prisoner in the course of him being detained
in the prison custody under section 78 of the Ordinance;
It may now, be examined.
It is in this backdrop of the case, I would think it pertinent at this juncture to
carefully, examine the scheme embodied in the Ordinance in general and the
provisions contained therein with regard to the constitution and powers of a
Prison Tribunal for punishment of prisoners for the offences stipulated
therein insofar as it would be necessary for the determination of the issue at
hand before us.
The preamble to the Ordinance states that, “It is an ordinance to amend and
consolidate the law relating to Prisons”.
Page 7 of 24
Part I of the Ordinance deals with the establishment and officers of the Prisons
and section 2 thereof, enacts thus;
“The prisons situated at the places mentioned in the Schedule shall he
or continue to be prisons for the reception of prisoners of every
description committed or remanded under the authority of any
court, having jurisdiction within any part of the districts or limits set
opposite the name of such places respectively in the said Schedule:
Provided always that it shall be lawful for the Minister, by Order, at any
time or from time to time to close any of the prisons mentioned in the
Schedule, or to make ay alteration in the districts or limits within which
any such prisons are appointed, and also to establish any other prison
or prisons for Sri Lanka or for any part thereof, and any such Order to
revoke, alter, or amend; and every prison so established shall become
subject to the provisions of this Ordinance in the same manner as if
such prison had been mentioned in the Schedule.” [Emphasis is mine]
A careful analysis of section 2 of the Ordinance, makes it clear that the
primary objective of the establishment of the Prisons is;
a) for the reception of prisoners of every description;
b) committed or remanded under the authority of any court;
[Emphasis is mine]
Hence, it becomes manifest that, Prisons are meant for the reception of
prisoners of every description. [Emphasis is mine]
This brings me to the next question, as to what kind of prisoners are meant
to be the prisoners so to be received by the Prisons as provided for by section
2 of the Ordinance?
It is only, and only, the prisoners who may be committed or remanded by
any Court under its the authority by way of a warrant of committal or a
Page 8 of 24
warrant of remand as provided for by section 2 of the Ordinance. [Emphasis
is mine]
in the light of Section 104 of the Ordinance, prisoners are of two kinds,
namely;
a) Civil prisoner.
b) Criminal prisoner.
Section 104 of the Ordinance defines “civil prisoner” to mean as follows;
a) judgment-debtor committed to prison under the Civil Procedure
Code; or
b) a person committed to prison under section 252 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure Act, No. 15 of 1979, in default of payment of
a fine imposed under that section of that Act; or
c) a person ordered to be detained in prison under section 390 of
the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, No. 15 of 1979; or
d) a person committed to prison under section 422 (4) of the Code
of Criminal Procedure Act, No 15 of 1979.; or
e) a person committed to prison for contempt of court, not being a
person sentenced -
i. to rigorous imprisonment for contempt of court;
ii. to simple or rigorous imprisonment as for a contempt
of court under section 449 (1) of the Code of Criminal
Procedure Act, No. 15 of 1979; or
f) a person committed to prison by order of a civil court under any
provision of written law which does not authorize a sentence of
rigorous imprisonment to be imposed”
Page 9 of 24
Section 104 of the Ordinance defines “criminal prisoner” to mean as follows;
“criminal prisoner " means any prisoner other than a civil prisoner”
Who then, is a criminal prisoner? Criminal Prisoner is a prisoner that may be
committed or remanded to a prison custody, by a Court by way of a warrant
of committal or a warrant of remand addressed to the Superintendent of
Prisons under the provisions of sections 115, 159, 239, 263, 286, 287, 289
and 290 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 as amended
etc.
A warrant of committal is mainly, three-fold, namely;
a) warrant of committal to remand;
b) warrant of committal to trial;
c) warrant of committal to sentence;
Hence, it becomes manifest that, a warrant of committal cannot be limited
only, to a kind of warrant of committals as stated in the submissions oral and
written by the learned Counsel for the Petitioner for; there may be any other
mode of warrant of committals too, under the law that may be issued by a
Court as enumerated above.
Section 78 of the Ordinance lists out the prison offences as follows;
“A prisoner shall be guilty of an offence against prison discipline if he -
(i) mutinies or incites another prisoner to mutiny;
(ii) assaults or uses criminal force on, or causes hurt or grievous hurt
to, a prison officer or another prisoner, or incites a fellow prisoner to
commit any such offence ;
(iii) fails or refuses to obey any lawful order of the Superintendent or of
any other prison officer or commits a breach of any prison regulation;
(iv) escapes or conspires to escape from lawful custody;
Page 10 of 24
(v) swears, curses, or uses any abusive, insulting, threatening or other
improper language or gesture;
(vi) is indecent in language, conduct, or gesture;
(vii) is impertinent, insubordinate or insolent in demeanor to any prison
officer or to any Visitor;
(viii) creates a disturbance or behaves in a disorderly manner ;
(ix) refuses to work, or willfully mismanages work, or fails to perform
his allotted task, or is idle, careless or negligent at work;
(x) willfully evades labour by self-disablement or by refusing to take food
or by feigning madness or illness or other incapacity for work;
(xi) willfully damages or disfigures any part of the prison, any prison
properly or any prison clothing or equipment;
(xii) is in possession of, or keeps in a cell or any other place any article
not permitted by the rules of the prison ;
(xiii) leaves a cell or other place of work or location without permission;
(xiv) gives to, or receives from, or exchanges with, any other prisoner
any article whatever without the permission of the Superintendent;
(xv) traffics or has any business dealings with any prison officer or with
any other person;
(xvi) without the authority of a prison officer, communicates whether by
writing, speech or gesture with any person who is not connected with
the administration of the prison ;
(xvii) gambles, or possesses any playing cards, dice or other instrument
or device for gambling ;
Page 11 of 24
(xviii) prefers a false charge against a prison officer or another prisoner
or incites any other prisoner to do so ;
(xix) makes groundless complaints or incites others to do so;
(xx) removes food from the place where meals are consumed, or
conceals food;
(xxi) commits any nuisance;
(xxii) bathes or washes at unauthorized places or times;
(xxiii) writes or receives any unauthorized letter or communication;
(xxiv) refuses when called upon to assist a prison officer in quelling a
mutiny or disturbance or in capturing any escaped or escaping
prisoner, or leaves his seat, working place or other location during a
mutiny or disturbance without an order from a prison officer;
(xxv) omits to give a warning or an alarm when it is known that a
prisoner is escaping or attempting to escape;
(xxvi) omits to give immediate information to the prison authorities
when he is aware of a design to commit an offence against the rules;
(xxvii) files, cuts or tampers with iron bars, locks or doors;
(xxviii) commits a breach of any rule or lawful order ; (xxix) offends in
any other way against the good order and discipline of the prison ;
(xxx) aids and abets another prisoner in committing or attempting to
commit any of the foregoing offences against prison discipline; or
(xxxi) attempts to commit any of the foregoing offences other than those
specified in paragraphs (iii), (v), (vii), (viii), (ix), (xii) (xix), (xxiv), (xxv),
and (xxvi).”
Page 12 of 24
A careful analysis of the list of offences makes it manifest that, offences listed
in section 78 of the Ordinance, are two-fold, namely;
a) offences of serious nature;
b) offences of trivial nature;
Section 81 of the Ordinance provides for the constitution and powers of the
tribunal for punishment of prisoners and it enacts thus;
“(1) (a) If any prisoner is charged with mutiny or incitement to mutiny,
or with escape or attempt to escape or abetment of escape from lawful
custody, or with causing hurt or grievous hurt to a prison officer or with
attempt to cause hurt or grievous hurt to a prison officer by means of
any instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument
which, when used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death; or
(b) if any prisoner is charged with any offence against prison
discipline which, in the opinion of the Superintendent or a Visitor
acting under section 79, is not adequately punishable by him or
is not adequately punishable under that section by reason of the
prisoner's record of previous convictions of offences against
prison discipline, the Superintendent shall in the former case,
and the Superintendent or Visitor may in the latter, cause the
offender to be tried by a Magistrate of the Division in which the
prison is situated and two Visitors who shall be members of the
Local Visiting Committee, unless for any reason no member of
that committee is able to serve on that tribunal.
(2) Every inquiry into a prison offence under this section shall be held
in the prison on such date not later than seven days after the receipt of
information of the offence from the Superintendent, as the Magistrate
may appoint:
Page 13 of 24
Provided that no delay beyond the aforesaid period of seven days shall
be deemed to invalidate any inquiry held under this section, if the
Magistrate certifies that the delay was due to a cause which, in his
opinion, is good and sufficient.
(3) Every Visitor summoned for the purpose of acting in a judicial
capacity under the provisions of this section shall attend at the prison
on the date and at the time specified unless prevented by illness or
other sufficient cause :
Provided that in the event of either or both of the Visitors summoned
failing so to attend, the Magistrate and the Visitor who is present or the
Magistrate alone, as the case may be, may perform all the functions and
exercise all the powers of the tribunal.
(4) The tribunal shall have power to inquire into the offence upon oath
or affirmation and by a majority verdict to punish the offender -
(a) with confinement in a punishment cell for any time not
exceeding one month ; or
(b) with any one of the several punishments a Superintendent is
authorized to impose under section 79; or
(c) with imprisonment of either description for a term not
exceeding five years in the case of the offence of escaping or
attempting to escape from lawful custody or the abetment of any
such offence and not exceeding six months in any other case;
(d) with a combination of any two of the above-mentioned
punishments.
(5) A term of imprisonment imposed under this section shall not run
concurrently with, but shall be in addition to, any term of imprisonment
Page 14 of 24
or of preventive detention which the offender may be undergoing at the
time of the inquiry.
(6) Any term of imprisonment imposed under any other written law on
an offender at any time while he is serving a term of imprisonment
imposed under this section, shall commence on the expiry of the term
of imprisonment imposed under this section.”
Upon a careful analysis of section 81 of the Ordinance in its totality, read in
conjunction with section 2 thereof, it becomes manifest that a Prison Tribunal
constituted thereunder, which consist of the Magistrate of the division in
which the prison is situated and two visitors who shall be members of the
local visiting committee, is vested with jurisdiction to try and determine any
offence as listed in section 78 of the Ordinance, which is committed “only”,
by a prisoner and as referred to it by the Superintendent of Prisons taking
into his consideration the gravity of the offence and inflict punishment upon
conviction; and that every inquiry into a prison offence as such shall be held
in the prison; and that Prison Tribunal shall have the power to inquire into
the offence upon oath or affirmation and by a majority verdict to punish the
offender inter-alia, with imprisonment of either description for a term not
exceeding five years in the case of an offence of escaping or attempting to
escape from lawful prison custody etc; and that there shall be no appeal from
a conviction or sentence under section 79 or section 81 of the Ordinance.
However, section 85 of the Ordinance preserves the jurisdiction of any
competent Court to hear and determine any charge in respect of an offence
punishable under the penal code or any other written law subject to the
exception contained in the proviso thereto and it enacts thus;
“Nothing contained in sections 79, 81, 82, 83, and 84 shall be deemed
to deprive any competent court in Sri Lanka, of its jurisdiction to hear
and determine any charge in respect of an offence punishable under
the Penal Code or any other written law:
Page 15 of 24
Provided, however, that no person shall be punished both under the
aforesaid sections and by a court for the same offence.”
In the light of the law enumerated above, it is beyond an iota of doubt that,
the Prison Tribunal so constituted under section 81 of the Ordinance has been
clothed with jurisdiction and/or power and/or authority so granted to it by
the Ordinance, to try “only” a person who is cloaked in the garb of a
prisoner within the definition assigned to it by section 104 of the
Ordinance as quoted above, for an offence listed under section 78 thereof,
and “only”, inflict punishment on a prisoner as such upon conviction.
This inevitably, follows that, the Prison Tribunal so constituted under section
81 of the Ordinance has not in any manner, been clothed with jurisdiction
and/or power and/or authority so granted to it by the Ordinance, to try a
person who is not cloaked in the garb of a prisoner within the definition
assigned to it by section 104 of the Ordinance as quoted above for an
offence listed under section 78 thereof, nor does it have any jurisdiction
and/or power and/or authority to convict and inflict punishment on a
prisoner as such nor does it have any jurisdiction and/or power and/or
authority to make an order remanding a person who is not coming within the
definition of “a Prisoner”, to the prison custody until final conclusion of the
inquiry and/or trial to be commenced or already commenced under the
provisions of the Ordinance in respect of an offence committed by a prisoner
during his detention in the prison custody inasmuch as the Law as it stands
today, once a prisoner ceases to be a prisoner by reason of him being admitted
to bail by a Court of competent jurisdiction and/or by reason of the Prisoner
being released from the prison upon completion of the sentence inflicted upon
him by a Court of competent jurisdiction, a Prison Tribunal will lose its
jurisdiction and/or power and/or authority over a prisoner as such for; a
prisoner as such cannot in law, be in any manner, considered a prisoner any
further for the purposes of the exercise of the jurisdiction and/or power
and/or authority vested in a Prison Tribunal to try a prisoner and inflict
Page 16 of 24
punishment on him upon conviction as provided for by section 81 of the
Ordinance to be read with section 78 thereof.
As observed above, situation as such would in law, arise in any event that the
prisoner being admitted to bail by an order of Court or else a prisoner being
released from a prison custody upon completion of the sentence imposed
upon him by a Court etc; for; both those instances, the warrant of committal
issued by Court to the Superintendent of Prisons conferring upon him power
or authority to keep the prisoner under physical custody, will become expired
and/or extinct and therefore, it would be of no force nor valid in law any longer
resulting in the person who is cloaked in the garb of a prisoner within the
definition assigned to it by section 104 of the Ordinance as quoted above,
being no longer a prisoner within the meaning of the Ordinance capable in
law, to be detained any further in the prison. [Emphasis is mine]
The resultant position would be that, if a person as such is detained in the
prison any further without a warrant of committal so issued by a Court, such
detention will no doubt, become illegal and/or unlawful in the eyes of the law
as rightly, contended by the learned Counsel for the Petitioner.
Applying the law as enumerated above to the facts of the instant application
when the impugned order (A2/R3) was made by the learned Prison Tribunal
on 20.06.2024 directing the Detenu who had then, been remanded by virtue
of the warrant of remand issued both by the learned Magistrate of Kesbewa
as well as the learned Magistrate Colombo in respect of the cases filed before
them against the Detenu as enumerated above, to be further, remanded until
final conclusion of the inquiry and/or trial commenced against the Detenu on
the offence of attempting to escape from the lawful custody of the prison as
listed under section 78 of the Ordinance, where he had been detained at the
relevant and material time, thus, rejecting the preliminary objection so raised
thereto, by the learned Counsel for the Detenu, the Detenu had already, been
admitted to bail both by the learned Magistrate of Kesbewa in his order dated
27.05.2024 (Y3), as well as by the learned Magistrate Colombo in his order
Page 17 of 24
dated 26.04.2023 (Y1) and therefore, the warrant of committal issued by the
respective Magistrate’s Courts remanding the Detenu, had totally, become
expired and/or extinct and therefore, no longer valid or in force in the eyes of
the law.
In the circumstances, it clearly, appears that, the Detenu could not have been
considered any longer, “a prisoner” within the meaning of section 104 of the
Ordinance since the date when the Detenu had been so admitted to bail by
Court as manifest from Y1 and Y3, which resulted in the order of the learned
Prison Tribunal (A2/R3) remanding the Detenu until final conclusion of the
inquiry and/or trial already commenced against him before it under section
81 of the Ordinance to be read with section 78 thereof, being totally, illegal
and/or unlawful and thus, a nullity ab initio for; it had been made by the
learned Prison Tribunal at a time when it had lost its jurisdiction and/or
power and/or authority vested in it by the law as morefully, set out above, to
make an order as such (A2/R3) inasmuch as although, the Detenu-who was
at the time of the commencement of the inquiry and/or trial into the offence
alleged to have been committed by him under section 81 of the Ordinance,
was a person who was cloaked in the garb of a prisoner within the
definition assigned to it by section 104 of the Ordinance, had upon him
being admitted to bail by the respective Magistrate Courts as enumerated
above, completely, changed and removed his cloak from the garb of a
prisoner to the garb of an ordinary citizen of this Country, thus, making
himself not amenable to the jurisdiction of the Prison Tribunal any longer as
rightly, contended by the learned Counsel for the Petitioner. [Emphasis is
mine]
It is in this context, it would be pertinent to quote a passage from Wade and
Forsyth (12th Edition) at page 27 as cited to us by the Petitioner in the
written submissions (WS7) to the following effect; “The simple proposition that
a public authority may not act outside its powers (ultra vires) might fitly, be
called the central principle of administrative law. The juristic basis of judicial
review is the doctrine ultra vires….”
Page 18 of 24
It was held by the Supreme Court in the decision in Patrick Lowe & Sons
and Others Vs. Commercial Bank of Ceylon LTD 2001 [1] SLR 280 at page
284, “It is a fundamental principle of law that a person who functions in terms
of statutory power vested in him is subject to an implied limitation that he
cannot exceed such power or authority. The ultra vires doctrine, now
recognized universally, evolved in England on this premise (vide Ashbury)
Railway Carriage & Iron Co. Ltd., vs. Hector Riche and the Attorney General
vs. The Great Eastern Railway.' It follows that what is not permitted by the
provisions of the enabling statute should be taken as forbidden and struck
down by Court as being in excess of authority.”
Hence, the central principle of administrative law is that, a public authority
may not act outside its powers (ultra vires).
In view of the above, the Prison Tribunal had clearly, acted outside its
jurisdiction and/or authority and/or powers vested in it by section 81 of the
Ordinance to be read with section 78 thereof, when it had proceeded to
remand the Detenu and continue with the inquiry and/or trial already
commenced by it against the Detenu in respect of the offence alleged to have
been committed by him under section 78 of the Ordinance notwithstanding
the fact that, the Detenu had already, been admitted to bail by the said
Magistrate’s Courts as manifest from Y1 and Y3 and therefore, the Detenu
had no longer been a prisoner within the meaning of section 104 of the
Ordinance and as such, the Detenu was not amenable to the jurisdiction of
the Prison Tribunal.
However, under those circumstances, all what the learned Prison Tribunal
ought to have done was to forthwith abate the proceedings with regard to the
inquiry and/or trial already, commenced against the Detenu and direct the
Superintendent of Prisons to forthwith take steps to prosecute the Detenu in
a Court of competent jurisdiction for the offence alleged to have been
committed by him under section 78 of the Ordinance in terms of the law,
Page 19 of 24
particularly, under section 219 of the Penal Code. However, the Prison
Tribunal had failed to do so.
I would therefore, hold the order impugned (A2/R3) is one made without
jurisdiction and therefore, one made in excess of the powers so vested in the
Prison Tribunal (ultra vires) and as such, a nullity ab inito, as rightly,
contended by the learned Counsel for the Petitioner.
Hence, I would hold that, the order impugned (A2/R3) is liable to be quashed
by a mandate in the nature of a writ of certiorari.
In the circumstances, the 1st and/or 2nd Respondent and/or their servants,
agents and/or any person acting under their authority had no authority
whatsoever, to detain the Detenu any further on the strength of the impugned
order of the learned Prison Tribunal (A2/R3) from the stage that the Detenu
had been admitted to bail as aforesaid, by the Magistrate Court.
Hence, I would hold that, a writ of mandamus would lie to compel the 1st
and/or 2nd Respondent and/or their servants, agents and/or any person
acting under their authority, on the order impugned (A2/R3) to release the
Detenu forthwith from the Prison Custody together with a writ of prohibition
prohibiting the 1st and/or 2nd Respondent and/or their servants, agents
and/or any person acting under their authority, from detaining the Detenu
on the purported authority of the impugned order (A2/R3) in the custody of
the Prison.
I would now, advert to the preliminary objection so raised by the 1st to 4th
Respondents in their joint written submissions that, the Petitioner lacks locus
standi, to institute the instant application.
The preliminary objection is based on the premise that, in view of the opinion
expressed by the Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist in the Medical Report (Y2)
to the effect that the Detenu is able to understand the nature of the charge
and he can understand the difference between pleading guilty and not guilty
following treatment; and that he can also instruct counsel and follow court
Page 20 of 24
proceedings; and that therefore, the Detenu is fit to plead & stand trial, the
Detenu was a person who is fit to plead and stand trial by himself and
therefore, there had been no necessity for the Petitioner to institute the
instant application seeking relief for the Detenu.
It may now, be examined.
It was inter-alia, held by the Supreme Court in Wijesiri vs. Siriwardena 1982
[1] SLR 171 that,
“To apply for a Writ of Mandamus, it is not necessary to have a personal
interest but it is sufficient if the applicant can show a genuine interest
in the matter complained of and that he comes before Court as a Public
spirited person, concerned to see that the law is obeyed in the interest
of all.”.
It was held by this Court in A. R. Perera and Others v Central Freight
Bureau of Sri Lanka and Another 2006 [1] SLR 83 at Pages 89 and 90,
“As Lord Denning noted in R v Inland Revenue Commissioners ex p.
National Federation of Self Employed and Small Business Ltd.,(6)
English Courts have orchestrated the generous view that "if there is
good ground for supposing that a government department or public
authority is transgressing the law, or is about to transgress it, in a way
which offends or injures thousands of her Majesty's subjects, then any
one of those offended or injured can draw it to the attention of the court
of law and seek to have the law enforced". In the course of his judgment
in the same case, Lord Diplock observed as follows "It would, in my
view, be a grave lacuna in our system of public law if a pressure group,
like the federation, or even a single public spirited tax payer, were
prevented by outdated technical rules of locus standi from bringing the
matter to the attention of court to vindicate the rule of law and get the
unlawful conduct stopped."
Page 21 of 24
The rationale for the expanding canvas of locus standi in the context of
certiorari and prohibition was explained by H. W. R. Wade -
Administrative Law (8th Edition) pages 362 to 363 in the following
words;
“The prerogative remedies, being of a 'public' character as
emphasized earlier, have always had more liberal rules about
standing than the remedies of private law. Prerogative remedies
are granted at the suit of the Crown, as the titles of the cases
show; and the Crown always has standing to take action against
public authorities, including its own ministers, who act or
threaten to act unlawfully. As Devlin J said: Orders of certiorari
and prohibition are concerned principally with public order, it
being the duty of the High Court to see that inferior courts confine
themselves to their own limited sphere". In the same sense Brett
J had said in an earlier case that the question in granting
prohibition "is not whether the individual suitor has or has not
suffered damage, but is, whether the royal prerogative has been
encroached upon by reason of the prescribed order of
administration of justice having been disobeyed". Consequently
the court is prepared to act at the instance of a mere stranger,
though it retains discretion to refuse to do so if it considers that
no good would be done to the public.”
Wade further goes on to observe at page 683 that "...the House of Lords
is clearly now determined to prevent technicalities from impeding
judicial review so as to protect illegalities and derelictions committed by
public authorities".
Sri Lankan Courts too have been quick to recognize standing of any
citizen to seek relief against public authorities that stray outside their
legitimate bounds.”
Page 22 of 24
It was inter-alia, held by this Court in the case in CA/WRIT/0440/2014-
Decided on 17.03.2021 at page 19 that, “Who can file a writ application?
The short answer is - any "person" (as defined in section 2(s) of the
Interpretation Ordinance) who has "sufficient interest" as opposed to the
outdated requirement of "personal interest" because of the element of "public
interest".”.
It was inter-alia, held by this Court in the decision in CA/WRIT/338/2009-
Decided on 28.05.2025 at page 12 that, “Learned Counsel for the 3rd
Respondent submits that the Petitioners have no locus standi to file this
application. I cannot agree. High technical objections regarding locus standi
have no place in modern administrative law. A writ application can be filed by
any person, as defined in section 2(s) of the Interpretation Ordinance, who
has "sufficient interest" in the matter, notwithstanding a lack of "personal
interest" because of the element of "public interest" involved in the subject
matter of controversy. The Petitioner in such an application can even be a
stranger. If the Petitioner comes to Court genuinely, as a public-spirited
citizen concerned to see that the law is obeyed in the interest of all, his
application shall be entertained. (Vide Lanka Viduli Podu Sevaka Sangamaya
v. Ceylon Electricity Board.”
Hence, the law as it stands today, with regard to the locus standi in an
application for a prerogative writ is that, a writ application can be filed by any
person, as defined in section 2(s) of the Interpretation Ordinance, who has
"sufficient interest" in the matter, notwithstanding a lack of "personal
interest" because of the element of "public interest" involved in the subject
matter of controversy. The Petitioner in such an application can even be a
stranger. If the Petitioner comes to Court genuinely, as a public-spirited
citizen concerned to see that the law is obeyed in the interest of all, his
application shall be entertained.
It appears from the averments in the Petition of the Petitioner that, he had
come to Court genuinely, as a public-spirited citizen concerned to see that the
Page 23 of 24
law is obeyed by the Prison Tribunal and the Prison Officials not only in the
interest of his son-the Detenu but also in the interest of all. Besides, it had
never been the position adverted to by the Respondents in the statement of
objections of the 1st to 4th Respondents or in the joint written submissions of
the 1st to 4th Respondents that it was not so.
I would therefore, hold that the Petitioner has come to Court genuinely, as a
public-spirited citizen concerned to see that the law is obeyed by the Prison
Tribunal and the Prison Officials not only in the interest of his son-the Detenu
but also in the interest of all.
Hence I would hold, that the Petitioner has sufficient interest to institute the
instant application.
I would therefore, proceed to overrule the preliminary objection so raised by
the 1st to 4th Respondents on the premise that, the Petitioner has no locus
standi to institute the instant application.
In view of all the above circumstances, I would hold that, the Petitioner had
established that, he is entitled to the relief as prayed for in prayer ‘b’, ‘c’ and
‘d’ of his petition.

d) a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Prohibition prohibiting the 1st
